title: The forty, closed
hookLine: forty ways to meditate, because no two people walk in the same door.
tomorrow: what makes a gift a good one: the size, or something else?

lines: ONE SNEAKER, A WALL OF SIZES.
cards: A shoe store stocks the same sneaker in a wall of sizes, and nobody calls that indecisive. Feet differ. So, forty ways to meditate: why so many?
Buddhaghosa's answer is the same as the shoe store's. Minds differ. A subject that steadies one person agitates the next.
Forty doors, he's saying, and one house behind them. The real question is the second half: which one is yours?

teach.b: Look back at the doors of the last forty days, in Buddhaghosa's own grouping. Ten kasinas: the earth disc, water, fire, air, colors, light, space. Ten kinds of foulness, the body after death.
Ten recollections: the Buddha, the teaching, the community, virtue, giving, the bright ones, death, the body, the breath, peace. Four divine abidings: kindness, compassion, gladness, equanimity.
Four formless states, ending in the one the Buddha walked away from.
Then one perception, food, and one defining, the four elements. Forty. And the manual doesn't ask anyone to do them all.

A teacher matches the subject to the person's temperament. For someone quick to anger, the divine abidings: warmth aimed straight at the trouble. For someone pulled by wanting, the foulness subjects and the body's parts.
For the restless, scattered mind, the breath.

teach.h: FITTED TO THE PERSON, NOT RANKED.
teach.b: The subjects aren't ranked; they're fitted.
Buddhaghosa's word for a subject is kammatthana, a place of work.
Which says something homely. A meditation subject isn't a trophy. It's a workbench, and the right one is the one at your height.

how: In Theravada meditation, as the Visuddhimagga describes it, a teacher chooses a subject suited to the student's temperament from the forty; a student may keep one main subject alongside short daily ones like the four protections.

o: the full set of meditation subjects, fitted to minds
forty rules every meditator promises to keep
forty days of retreat a monk keeps once a year

games.q: the forty, in Buddhaghosa's groups — tap the pairs.
p: the earth disc, water, fire, air and more
the Buddha, death, the breath, peace

s: you're meant to practice all forty subjects
the manual has a teacher fit one subject to the person's temperament. the forty are doors, not a checklist.
the divine abidings for someone quick to anger; foulness for someone pulled by wanting; the breath for a scattered mind.
breathing is the only real Buddhist meditation
the breath is one of the forty, suited to some minds. none is ranked above the others.

games.q: your friend tried the death reflection and it left her anxious for days. what would a teacher following Buddhaghosa most likely do?
o: tell her to push through: the hard subject is the best one.
fit her to another subject that suits her temperament.
tell her meditation clearly isn't for her and to stop.
games.why: the subjects are fitted, not ranked. a teacher's job in the manual is to find the door that suits the person.

practice: Out of the forty, pick the one that has stayed with you: the earth disc, the breath, kindness, the meal's journey, the four on your hand. Say its name once, quietly.
Then give it the whole sit, the way you'd settle in at your own workbench.

wordCard.voice: The forty: Buddhaghosa's full set of meditation subjects, from the earth disc to the four elements. Many doors, fitted to many minds, one house.

orig.note: Pali: a place of work, the word for a meditation subject.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: forty doors, and one of them was cut for you. Forty of forty: the block is closed.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 3 (the forty meditation subjects by group: ten kasinas, ten kinds of foulness, ten recollections, four divine abidings, four immaterial states, one perception, one defining; their suitability to the six temperaments: e.g. the divine abidings for the hating temperament, foulness and the body for the greedy, mindfulness of breathing for the deluded and speculative; kammatthana as the term for a subject)
